chapter_theme: Having failed to terrify the sage Munichandran, Neelakesi takes the form of the princess Kamalekai and tries to seduce him; he sees through her, answers her feigned fears and wiles, and when she weeps over her birth begins a sermon on birth, the four states of birth, the seven hells and the grading of beings by their number of senses.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Jain sage whose penance Neelakesi cannot break
the troops who sing and dance as Neelakesi worships in her disguise

57.reading: Seeing that the sage's power is such that the fire of his austerity would destroy her and there is no way to counter it, the demoness of Death-like cruelty drops her rage, humbled, and bows, praying that her cruel deeds be quenched.
57.nuance: The verse names the sage by his ஆற்றல் (power) and her by Death, கூற்றம்: the contest is staged as austerity against death. Whether the bow is already pretence is left open; the next verse shows her planning a feigned worship with the same kind of plea.
57.event: Neelakesi, unable to frighten the sage, ends her rage and bows to him, asking that her cruel karma be quenched.

58.reading: She reasons that if she takes the shape of a young woman and, under cover of a feigned worship that prays for her old bound deeds to perish, breaks his inner restraint in that shape, he will abandon his fire-like vow.
58.nuance: The plan turns the language of release from karma (பழவினை கெடுக) into bait: the plea a penitent would make is to be her disguise. Her target is named precisely: not his body but his மனநிறை, the containment of his mind.
58.event: Neelakesi resolves to take a young woman's form and break the sage's vow through feigned worship.

59.reading: At the end of the night she appears in the very form of Kamalekai, the king's only daughter, radiant as the goddess of fortune, and goes with garlands, sandal paste and cool flowers to worship.
59.nuance: She borrows a real person's form, the king's daughter, so the deceit also puts a princess's good name at risk. Line 4's words of praise (சேமம் காவல சேவடி போற்று) may be addressed to the shrine's guardian; who they address is not plain.
59.event: Neelakesi appears in the form of the princess Kamalekai and sets out with offerings to worship.

60.reading: As she bows, circles the place and worships, troops sing the praises due and dance the thunangai while her girdle sways under her garment, and she, in her lovely form, resolves to approach the ascetic.
60.nuance: Who the கணங்கள் are, her own spirit retinue playing attendants or the shrine's troops, is not said.
60.event: Neelakesi worships at the shrine while troops sing and dance, then resolves to go near the sage.

61.reading: Standing where the famed ascetic can hear, she orders the guards to stop at the gate and come no further, the servants to see to what is needed, and her people to come close when she has some want.
61.nuance: The speech is played for the overhearing sage: a princess's orders to her household are her credentials. Line 3 (கூலி யான் குறை உளது) is obscure.
61.event: Neelakesi, as the princess, dismisses her guards and servants within earshot of the sage.

62.reading: Coming to the shrine, she bows to the great ascetic seated at the foot of a broad-leaved banyan and prays that her cruel deeds be quenched, she who wears the wondrous shining form she had wished for.
62.nuance: Line 3 repeats the plea of verse 57 almost word for word (என்செய் கருவினை தணிக்க), now spoken through a borrowed body as a lure.
62.event: Neelakesi, disguised, bows to the sage under the banyan and asks that her karma be quenched.

63.reading: Bearing a desired and desire-making form, the beauty of a young woman, and giving no thought at all to the nature of the lord rich in virtues, she stands like a creeper beside a tall creeper and asks the sage of full austerity for his grace.
63.nuance: The simile of a creeper by a creeper puts her as clinging to him; the verse stresses that the form is both chosen (வேண்டிய) and made to rouse desire (வேட்கைசெய்).
63.event: Neelakesi stands close beside the sage in her borrowed form and asks for his grace.

64.reading: The sage, who knows the scriptural way that cuts the many deeds bound up in the soul's union with and difference from the body, steadies his yoga and says that this woman is a deceiver and no king's daughter at all.
64.nuance: ஒற்றுமை வேற்றுமை, the body and soul as one and as other, may be the Jain view that they are one in one respect and distinct in another; that is my reading. Line 3, where he speaks (பணிந்தவரட் காசிடை), is obscure, so it is unclear whether he says it to her, to himself or aside.
64.event: The sage, fixed in yoga, perceives that the woman is a deceiver and not the princess.

claims.claim: the way of the scripture cuts the many deeds that cling to the soul through its entanglement with the body

65.reading: When the sage asks why she has come, the golden lady, her ornaments clinking like a parrot's chatter, says she has come to pay what is due for boons she once prayed for.
65.event: Asked why she has come, Neelakesi says she has come to fulfil vows for boons granted.

66.reading: Asked what boon she sought, she says it was that the king of a hostile land not rise unlawfully against her father, with flowers, sandal, oblation and incense for the god, and the knowing sage answers that if so, her words are fair.
66.nuance: The sage's reply (உரை அழகு ஈது) can be plain assent or a dry remark on a well-made story; he already knows she is not the princess.
66.event: Neelakesi names a vow for her father's safety from a hostile king, and the sage comments on her answer.

67.reading: With a jewel on one ear, a makara earring swinging on the other, bees humming and gems flashing, she says the fear such tender women speak of is great indeed, and that whatever others feel, this forest troubles her.
67.nuance: The demoness of the burning ground claims to be afraid of her own haunt.
67.event: Neelakesi, in her finery, tells the sage that the forest frightens her.

68.reading: The sage answers that if she were the daughter of the king of the jewelled crown and fierce spear she would be playing with her companions and sitting among her kin, and that this disease-ridden demon forest is hard for any to enter except those who have renounced with resolve.
68.nuance: He tests her story against what a princess's life would be, without accusing her outright.
68.event: The sage questions why a king's daughter would come into a demon forest that only renouncers approach.

69.reading: With bamboo and such things, she says, the great forest is a wonder, yet hard to bear, a demon forest full of afflictions; and with her hair on end she asks the great sage whether he has seen any of the forms that are hard to see.
69.event: Neelakesi, feigning fear, asks the sage whether he has seen the spirits of the forest.

70.reading: The sage answers that those who live together in one house see each other come and go, and mother and children do not take fright at one another; for those who know the many states of birth and the truth of souls such fear is rare, and even if these beings exist it is not fitting for him to speak of them.
70.nuance: The beings he declines to speak of stand before him; his refusal can be read as tact toward one he has already seen through. The housemates image makes all souls kin in one dwelling, across the states of birth.

claims.claim: one who knows the states of birth and the nature of souls does not fear other beings, who are like housemates and kin

71.reading: When the sage has spoken, the tender one asks him to teach her with his whole mind a mantra, if there is one, so that deaths cannot reach her; the ascetic whom even the sky-dwellers worship answers that they will not reach her though Indra himself wished it, so what are demons.
71.nuance: It is unclear whether அவை (line 3) are the deaths she fears or the spirits; either way the assurance is ironic, given to the demoness herself.
71.event: Neelakesi asks the sage for a mantra against death, and he tells her no such harm will reach her.

72.reading: She makes her coral lip tremble, loosens the garment at her hips, draws in her breasts, flashes her rain-dark eyes and sways her slender waist, and as she does all this he asks what any of it is to him.
72.nuance: The seduction ends in one line of indifference: he does not argue against desire, he finds nothing in it addressed to him.
72.event: Neelakesi plays every wile of seduction, and the sage asks what these are to him.

73.reading: Her gold earrings and white bangles slipping, the flowers falling from her head to the ground and tears streaming from her long eyes, she says her anguish is great and cries out that this birth may perish.
73.nuance: The text does not say whether the grief is one more ruse or the first real turn; the sage answers it as real, with a sermon on birth.
73.event: Neelakesi breaks down weeping and wishes her present birth would end.

74.reading: The high ascetic tells her that if she wishes to hear of birth, of the diseases born within birth, of the medicine of dharma that cuts them and of that medicine's excellence, she should set her mind on dharma, cease her wavering and her actions, grow still and sit, and she sits.
74.event: The sage offers to teach birth and its cure, and Neelakesi sits down to listen.

claims.claim: birth is the ground of disease and dharma is the medicine that cuts it

75.reading: Of the four states of birth he begins with the hell-dwellers: the hell lands, held up by three rings of wind, lie below the nigoda, and are named darkness upon darkness, darkness, smoke, mire, sand, sharp gravel and gems.
75.nuance: The seven names, read upward from the lowest, match the Jain list of seven hell-earths (deepest darkness, darkness, smoke, mud, sand, gravel, gem). How line 3 should be divided (நிகோதத்தின் இம்பர் இருளின் இருள் இருள்) is my reading.

claims.claim: living beings are born into four states of birth, of which hell is one
the hell-earths lie below, borne up by three rings of wind

76.reading: These seven spread into eighty-four hundred thousand, with the varieties of their pits; the beings below are sexless and of shapes beyond counting, born there as their lot.
76.nuance: Lines 3 and 4 (முழுச்செவி கிண்ணர்கள், முவ்வாதம் அல்லார்) are hard to construe; I read அலிகள் as the hell-dwellers being neither male nor female, which Jain teaching holds, but the line may list other kinds of being.

claims.claim: the seven hells open into eighty-four hundred thousand dwellings
the beings of hell are neither male nor female

77.reading: If she wishes him to tell the kinds of animal life too, he says, they are of two sorts, those that stand fixed in the earth and those that move, and the fixed ones are of five kinds throughout this world.
77.nuance: Here 'animal' (விலங்கு) covers the whole state of non-human, non-divine, non-hell life, down to the fixed beings.

claims.claim: beings of the animal state are either fixed or moving, and the fixed are of five kinds

78.reading: The moving ones, found in this middle world, have from two to five senses; among them the snail and the like, which lack a nose and have only taste beyond touch, are two-sensed.

claims.claim: moving beings have from two to five senses, and creatures like the snail have only two

79.reading: Lice, mites, ants and the like, countless millions, have those two senses and smell, three in all; those lacking hearing, like the wasp and the honeybee, have four.

claims.claim: insects like lice and ants have three senses, and bees and wasps, which lack hearing, have four

links.note: Both set the ascetic's ஆற்றல் against கூற்றம்: the Kural says those who gain the power of penance can leap even Death; here a demoness likened to Death owns that the fire of the sage's penance would destroy her.
links.teaches: The couplet's abstract boast that penance outruns death becomes a scene in which Death's likeness itself gives up the fight, and the victory comes without the ascetic acting at all.

gains.a: the demoness's surrender is read as the outcome the Kural promised for true penance
gains.b: the couplet's claim gains a dramatised instance in which the threat is a being, not the end of life

links.note: Verse 58's plan that the sage will drop his vow once she breaks his restraint in a woman's form meets its answer in 72, where every wile draws only the question of what these are to him.
links.teaches: Holding the plan beside its failure shows that the epic places the vow's safety in the sage's inner containment, the very மனநிறை she meant to break, not in avoiding the temptress.

links.note: Both heroines of the debate epics take another woman's form: Neelakesi takes a princess's shape to break a sage's vow, Manimekalai took Kayachandigai's shape to teach her former husband birth and death and end his karma.
links.teaches: The Jain and Buddhist epics use the same device of a borrowed body to opposite ends, one to bind a man in desire and one to free him from it, so the borrowed form itself is neutral and the intent decides.

links.note: The Kural calls the tie of body and life a friendship that ends as a bird leaves its nest; the Neelakesi's sage knows a scripture that cuts the deeds entangled in the soul's oneness with and difference from the body.
links.teaches: Set beside the Kural, the Jain verse turns the body-soul tie from a bond death simply ends into a knot of deeds that a discipline can cut while one still lives.

gains.a: the sage's knowledge is placed against the Tamil commonplace of body and life as passing companions
gains.b: the couplet's bird-and-nest friendship gains a doctrinal account of what holds the two together

links.note: Both picture life in a house: the Kural asks whether life, a lodger in the body, has no home of its own; the Neelakesi's sage likens beings across the states of birth to people who live together in one house and do not fear each other.
links.teaches: The same lodging image serves the Kural to make the soul homeless and the Jain sage to make all souls housemates, so it can teach unrest or fearlessness depending on whether one looks at one body or at all lives.

gains.a: the sage's housemates image is seen to rework a known Tamil figure of the soul as a lodger
gains.b: the couplet's lonely lodger gains a counter-image in which every being shares the house

links.note: The Naladiyar answers a beautiful woman's appeal by dissecting the body into entrails, blood and bone and asking which part is she; the Neelakesi's sage meets a full display of wiles with one question, what are these to us.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar's dissection is a method for one still tempted, while the sage needs no method; and since this beauty is a demoness's borrowed shape, the Naladiyar's question of where the woman is in the body has, here, a literal answer: nowhere.

gains.a: the sage's bare dismissal is shown to stand where a quatrain needs a whole argument
gains.b: the quatrain's rhetorical question gains a scene in which the alluring body truly belongs to no woman

links.note: Both call birth a sickness with a medicine: the Neelakesi's sage names the medicine as dharma that cuts the diseases of birth; Pattinathar names it as never forgetting the lotus feet of the Lord of the Tillai hall.
links.teaches: The two traditions agree on the diagnosis and part on the cure: the Jain medicine is a dharma one takes up oneself with no god named, while the Siddhar's medicine is remembrance of the Lord's feet.

gains.a: the Jain sermon's medicine is set against a Saiva one, showing that it names no saviour
gains.b: the Siddhar's medicine of the feet is seen as one answer among rival cures for the same disease

links.note: The Neelakesi's sage counts four states of birth (நாற்கதி); Aravanar in the Manimekalai counts six kinds of living beings: humans, gods, Brahmas, hell-beings, animals and ghosts.
links.teaches: The rival epics disagree even on how many destinies there are, so a reader comparing their karma teaching must first map the Jain four gatis onto the Buddhist six realms.

links.note: The Neelakesi's sage says the hells are seven (ஏழாய்) and spread into eighty-four hundred thousand dwellings; the Manimekalai's goddess summons the eight kinds of hell-beings (எண் வகை நரகர்) within the Chakravala.
links.teaches: The two epics count the hells differently, seven earths stacked below the world against eight kinds of hell-dwellers within one world-system, so hell's shape is itself a point of sectarian difference.

new_concepts.gloss: the vow; a religious observance or discipline undertaken
new_concepts.label_source: the verse's own word: தீநிகர் நோன்பு (58)

new_concepts.gloss: a state or course of birth: in Jain teaching one of the four (hell, animal, human, god) into which deeds carry a soul
new_concepts.label_source: the verses' own words: பல் கதிகள் (70), நாற்கதி (75)

new_concepts.gloss: a sense faculty; in Jain teaching beings are graded by how many of the five senses they have

source_issues: Verse 64 is printed with the number 6; it is read as 64, since the next verse is 65.
Verse 61, line 3 (கூலி யான்குறை யுளதெனக்) is obscure and may be corrupt.
Verse 64, line 3 (பணிந்தவரட் காசிடை) does not divide cleanly; the phrase that says to whom the sage speaks is unclear.
Verse 76, lines 3-4 (முழுச்செவி கிண்ணர்கள், முவ்வாதம் அல்லார்) are hard to construe and may be corrupt.
Verse 71, line 4 ends with a stray semicolon in the text.
